def-hh-hecke-symmetry-and-ordered-basis-.definition_or_statement_exact:
Let $F=\mathbb Q(q)$, where $q$ is an indeterminate, let $N\ge1$, and let $V_N$ have ordered basis $e_1<\cdots<e_N$. Put $c=q-q^{-1}$. Define $T\in\operatorname{End}_F(V_N\otimes V_N)$ by

$$T(e_a\otimes e_b)=\begin{cases}q\,e_a\otimes e_a,&a=b,\\ e_b\otimes e_a,&a<b,\\ e_b\otimes e_a+c\,e_a\otimes e_b,&a>b.\end{cases}$$

For an invertible operator $R$ on $V_N\otimes V_N$, the phrase **Hecke symmetry of normalized parameter $q$** means that the operators $R_1=R\otimes1$ and $R_2=1\otimes R$ on $V_N^{\otimes3}$ satisfy $R_1R_2R_1=R_2R_1R_2$, and that $(R-qI)(R+q^{-1}I)=0$. This is a property in the definition, not an assertion that every invertible operator has it. The next item proves that the displayed $T$ has this property.

The alternative generator $S=qT$ has parameter $Q=q^2$ and satisfies $(S-QI)(S+I)=0$ whenever $T$ satisfies its normalized quadratic relation. At $q=1$ the displayed $T$ is the ordinary flip. At $q=-1$ the quadratic relation becomes $T^2=I$, while the displayed operator is not the ordinary flip.

lem-hh-type-a-tensor-operator-is-a-hecke.definition_or_statement_exact: For every $N\ge1$, the operator $T$ of [[def-hh-hecke-symmetry-and-ordered-basis-operator]] is invertible, satisfies $(T-qI)(T+q^{-1}I)=0$, and satisfies the adjacent braid identity $T_1T_2T_1=T_2T_1T_2$ on $V_N^{\otimes3}$. Its inverse is $T^{-1}=T-cI$, where $c=q-q^{-1}$. If $S=qT$ and $Q=q^2$, then $(S-QI)(S+I)=0$ and $S_1S_2S_1=S_2S_1S_2$. At $q=1$, $T$ specializes to the ordinary flip; at $q=-1$ its quadratic relation specializes to $T^2=I$, but the operator itself is not the ordinary flip.
lem-hh-type-a-tensor-operator-is-a-hecke.facts_and_assumptions_exact:
**Given:** $F=\mathbb Q(q)$, the ordered basis $e_1<\cdots<e_N$, the operator $T$ and $c=q-q^{-1}$ from [[def-hh-hecke-symmetry-and-ordered-basis-operator]].

[F1] The formula for $T$ on each ordered basis pair is the three-case formula in [[def-hh-hecke-symmetry-and-ordered-basis-operator]].

[F2] The elementary tensors $e_a\otimes e_b$ and $e_a\otimes e_b\otimes e_d$ form bases of the corresponding finite tensor powers, so equality on these vectors proves equality of linear maps ([[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]], [[thm-tensor-product-basis-from-bases]]).
lem-hh-type-a-tensor-operator-is-a-hecke.proof_exact:
**Given:** The data in [F1]–[F2].

1.1 For $a<b$, the span of $e_a\otimes e_b,e_b\otimes e_a$ is $T$-invariant and, in that ordered basis, $T$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&c\end{pmatrix}$; hence $T^2=cT+I$ there. On $e_a\otimes e_a$ one has $T=qI$ and $q^2=cq+1$. These subspaces partition the basis of $V_N\otimes V_N$, so $T^2-cT-I=0$ on the whole space. Since $T(T-cI)=(T-cI)T=I$, it is invertible with inverse $T-cI$, and $T^2-cT-I=(T-qI)(T+q^{-1}I)$ by expansion. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Write $abc$ for $e_a\otimes e_b\otimes e_c$. For distinct letters assume $a<b<c$, and for two letters assume $a<b$. Applying the three-case rule [F1] gives the same value for $T_1T_2T_1$ and $T_2T_1T_2$ in all thirteen weak-order patterns: $aaa\mapsto q^3aaa$; $aab\mapsto qbaa$; $aba\mapsto qaba+qc\,baa$; $baa\mapsto qaab+qc\,aba+q^2c\,baa$; $abb\mapsto qbba$; $bab\mapsto qbab+qc\,bba$; $bba\mapsto qabb+qc\,bab+q^2c\,bba$; $abc\mapsto cba$; $acb\mapsto bca+c\,cba$; $bac\mapsto cab+c\,cba$; $bca\mapsto acb+c\,bca+c\,cab+c^2cba$; $cab\mapsto bac+c\,bca+c\,cab+c^2cba$; and $cba\mapsto abc+c\,acb+c\,bac+c^2bca+c^2cab+(c+c^3)cba$. The first seven entries cover one or two distinct labels, and the last six cover all orders of three distinct labels. Thus the two braid composites agree on the tensor basis [F2] and hence on the whole tensor cube. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The normalized quadratic relation in step 1.1 gives $(qT-q^2I)(qT+I)=q^2(T-qI)(T+q^{-1}I)=0$; multiplying the braid identity of step 1.2 by $q^3$ on both sides gives the braid identity for $S=qT$. At $q=1$, $c=0$ and each branch of the formula is the flip, including the equal-label branch. At $q=-1$, $c=0$ and the quadratic relation is $T^2=I$, while $T(e_a\otimes e_a)=-e_a\otimes e_a$, so it is not the ordinary flip. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

thm-hh-hecke-symmetry-tensor-power-actio.definition_or_statement_exact: Let $F=\mathbb Q(q)$, $N\ge1$, and $n\ge0$. Let $H_n(F,q)$ be the type-A Hecke algebra generated by $t_1,\ldots,t_{n-1}$ with braid relations and $(t_i-q)(t_i+q^{-1})=0$; put $H_0=H_1=F$. On $V_N^{\otimes n}$ define $T_i$ by applying the operator of [[def-hh-hecke-symmetry-and-ordered-basis-operator]] in positions $i,i+1$. There is a unital algebra homomorphism $\rho_n:H_n(F,q)\to\operatorname{End}_F(V_N^{\otimes n})$ with $\rho_n(t_i)=T_i$. Its matrices are regular at $q=1$, where $T_i$ is the transposition of tensor positions $i,i+1$. This is an action into an endomorphism algebra; it makes no assertion that $\rho_n$ is injective.
thm-hh-hecke-symmetry-tensor-power-actio.facts_and_assumptions_exact:
**Given:** $F=\mathbb Q(q)$, $N\ge1$, $n\ge0$, and the normalized type-A Hecke presentation.

[F1] The presentation of $H_n$ is the specialization of the universal Coxeter Hecke presentation in [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]] with type $A_{n-1}$ and common parameter $q$.

[F2] The universal presentation has the usual quotient universal property; [[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]] proves its standard basis and its base-change compatibility.

[F3] The operator of [[lem-hh-type-a-tensor-operator-is-a-hecke-symmetry]] satisfies the quadratic and braid relations, and at $q=1$ it is the flip.
thm-hh-hecke-symmetry-tensor-power-actio.proof_exact:
**Given:** The data in [F1]–[F3].

1.1 For $n\ge2$, each $T_i$ satisfies $(T_i-qI)(T_i+q^{-1}I)=0$ by [F3]. Adjacent operators satisfy the braid relation because, on the three positions they meet, this is exactly the identity $T_1T_2T_1=T_2T_1T_2$ proved in [F3]; tensoring with identities on the other positions preserves that equality. If $|i-j|>1$, then $T_i$ and $T_j$ act on disjoint tensor factors, so on every elementary tensor each changes only its own pair and the two orders of application give the same tensor and coefficient. Thus the family $(T_i)$ satisfies every defining relation in [F1]. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 By the quotient universal property in [F2], the assignment $t_i\mapsto T_i$ extends uniquely to a unital $F$-algebra homomorphism $\rho_n$. For $n=0,1$ the algebra and endomorphism image are the scalar algebra and the unique unital map supplies the same conclusion. Each matrix entry of every $T_i$ is a Laurent polynomial in $q$, so it is regular at $q=1$; [F3] identifies the specialized operators as adjacent flips. The standard-basis theorem in [F2] concerns the abstract algebra and does not identify it with its image under $\rho_n$. [step 1.1, F2, F3] ∎

def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-.definition_or_statement_exact:
Let $F=\mathbb Q(q)$ with $q$ an indeterminate, let $N\ge1$, and put $K_i=L_iL_{i+1}^{-1}$ for $1\le i<N$. Start with the free associative $F$-algebra on $L_j,L_j^{-1}$ ($1\le j\le N$) and $E_i,F_i$ ($1\le i<N$), and quotient by the two-sided ideal generated by the following relations:

1. $L_jL_j^{-1}=L_j^{-1}L_j=1$ and $L_jL_k=L_kL_j$ for all $j,k$.
2. $L_jE_iL_j^{-1}=q^{\delta_{j,i}-\delta_{j,i+1}}E_i$ and $L_jF_iL_j^{-1}=q^{-\delta_{j,i}+\delta_{j,i+1}}F_i$.
3. $[E_i,F_j]=\delta_{ij}(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$.
4. $[E_i,E_j]=[F_i,F_j]=0$ when $|i-j|>1$.
5. For $|i-j|=1$, $E_i^2E_j-(q+q^{-1})E_iE_jE_i+E_jE_i^2=0$ and $F_i^2F_j-(q+q^{-1})F_iF_jF_i+F_jF_i^2=0$.

Here $[x,y]=xy-yx$. The free algebra and quotient construction are those of [[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]; this definition asserts existence of the presented associative algebra, not the well-definedness of structural maps on its quotient.

On $V_N$ with ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_N$, prescribe the candidate matrices
$$L_je_a=q^{\delta_{ja}}e_a,\qquad E_ie_a=\delta_{a,i+1}e_i,\qquad F_ie_a=\delta_{a,i}e_{i+1}.$$
Prescribe candidate coproduct and counit values by
$$\Delta(L_j)=L_j\otimes L_j,\quad \Delta(E_i)=E_i\otimes K_i+1\otimes E_i,\quad \Delta(F_i)=F_i\otimes1+K_i^{-1}\otimes F_i,$$
and $\epsilon(L_j^{\pm1})=1$, $\epsilon(E_i)=\epsilon(F_i)=0$. The following relation-descent lemma proves that these assignments define the vector representation and bialgebra structure, and hence the tensor actions used below.

lem-hh-quantum-presentation-and-tensor-a.definition_or_statement_exact: For the presented algebra $U_N$ and candidate assignments in [[def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-centralizers]], the matrices on $V_N$ satisfy every defining relation. The coproduct assignments descend to a coassociative algebra homomorphism $\Delta:U_N\to U_N\otimes_FU_N$ and the counit assignments descend to an algebra homomorphism $\epsilon:U_N\to F$ satisfying both counit identities. Consequently every tensor power $V_N^{\otimes n}$ has the action obtained by iterating $\Delta$; all its generator matrices have entries in $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$.
lem-hh-quantum-presentation-and-tensor-a.facts_and_assumptions_exact:
**Given:** $F=\mathbb Q(q)$, $N\ge1$, the algebra presentation and candidate maps in [[def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-centralizers]].

[F1] A free associative algebra modulo the two-sided ideal of its displayed relations is a presented algebra, and assignments descend exactly when they annihilate every defining relation ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]).

[F2] The tensor product of algebras has multiplication $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=ac\otimes bd$, and maps agreeing on the displayed generators agree on the presented algebra ([[thm-tensor-product-of-algebras-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[lem-hh-universal-presentations-and-base-change]]).

[F3] For $a_{ij}=2\delta_{ij}-\delta_{i,j+1}-\delta_{i+1,j}$, the defining $L$-weight relations imply $K_iE_jK_i^{-1}=q^{a_{ij}}E_j$ and $K_iF_jK_i^{-1}=q^{-a_{ij}}F_j$; in particular $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$, $a_{ii}=2$, and $a_{ij}=-1$ for adjacent indices.
lem-hh-quantum-presentation-and-tensor-a.proof_exact:
**Given:** The data in [F1]–[F3].

1.1 On $V_N$, each $L_j$ is diagonal and invertible, and the $L_j$ commute. Conjugating the matrix unit $E_i:e_{i+1}\mapsto e_i$ by $L_j$ multiplies its sole nonzero entry by $q^{\delta_{j,i}-\delta_{j,i+1}}$; conjugating $F_i:e_i\mapsto e_{i+1}$ gives the inverse exponent. Also $K_i$ has eigenvalue $q$ on $e_i$, $q^{-1}$ on $e_{i+1}$ and $1$ on every other basis vector, so $(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ is the diagonal matrix with entries $1,-1,0$ in those positions. Directly, $[E_i,F_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $[E_i,F_i]$ is that diagonal matrix. Products $E_iE_j$ and $E_jE_i$ (and the corresponding $F$ products) both vanish when $|i-j|>1$; $E_i^2=F_i^2=0$, and each middle three-letter Serre product also vanishes because its matrix-unit indices do not compose. Thus every defining relation holds, and the quotient universal property [F1] gives the vector representation. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Define $\Delta$ on the free generators by the displayed formulas in [[def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-centralizers]]. The $\Delta(L_j)$ are mutually commuting units with the displayed inverses. Conjugation by $\Delta(L_j)$ gives the required weights on each of the two terms of $\Delta(E_i)$ and $\Delta(F_i)$, since each $K_i$ is a Laurent monomial in the commuting $L$'s. For any $i,j$, expansion gives $[\Delta(E_i),\Delta(F_j)]=[E_i,F_j]\otimes K_i+K_j^{-1}\otimes[E_i,F_j]+[E_i\otimes K_i,K_j^{-1}\otimes F_j]$. The last cross term is zero: its first product can be reordered as $q^{a_{ji}-a_{ij}}K_j^{-1}E_i\otimes F_jK_i=K_j^{-1}E_i\otimes F_jK_i$, which is its reverse product by [F3]. If $i\ne j$, the remaining terms vanish; if $i=j$, they sum to $\bigl(K_i\otimes K_i-K_i^{-1}\otimes K_i^{-1}\bigr)/(q-q^{-1})=\Delta\bigl((K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})\bigr)$. For $|i-j|>1$, $a_{ij}=0$ and the $K_i$ commute with $E_j,F_j$; expanding the two commutators therefore proves that the distant $E$ and $F$ relations are preserved. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.3 Let $\gamma=q+q^{-1}$ and $S_{ij}(X,Y)=X^2Y-\gamma XYX+YX^2$ for adjacent $i,j$. For the $E$ relation write $\Delta(E_s)=A_s+B_s$ with $A_s=E_s\otimes K_s$, $B_s=1\otimes E_s$. In each of the three words $iij,iji,jii$, choose an $A$ at each selected position and a $B$ at each other position, then move the selected $K$ factors to the right using $K_rE_s=q^{a_{rs}}E_sK_r$. Grouping the resulting 24 terms by the number of selected positions gives: degree $0$ in the first factor is $1\otimes S_{ij}(E_i,E_j)$; degree $3$ is $S_{ij}(E_i,E_j)\otimes K_i^2K_j$; degree $1$ has respective coefficients $q+q^{-1}-\gamma$, $q^2+1-\gamma q$, $1+q^{-2}-\gamma q^{-1}$ on $E_i\otimes E_iE_jK_i$, $E_i\otimes E_jE_iK_i$, $E_j\otimes E_i^2K_j$; degree $2$ has respective coefficients $q^{-2}+1-\gamma q^{-1}$, $q^2+1-\gamma q$, $q+q^{-1}-\gamma$ on $E_i^2\otimes E_jK_i^2$, $E_iE_j\otimes E_iK_iK_j$, $E_jE_i\otimes E_iK_jK_i$. All six mixed coefficients are zero by the definition of $\gamma$, and the two pure terms vanish by the defining Serre relation. Thus $\Delta$ preserves every positive Serre relation. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The assignment $\phi(L_j)=L_j^{-1}$, $\phi(E_i)=F_i$, $\phi(F_i)=E_i$ preserves the presentation: it exchanges the two weight relations, sends the mixed commutator to its negative with $K_i$ replaced by $K_i^{-1}$, and exchanges the distant and Serre relations. It is an involution. On generators $\Delta(F_i)=\tau(\phi\otimes\phi)\Delta(E_i)$, where $\tau(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x$ is an algebra isomorphism. Since step 1.3 proves that the positive Serre polynomial maps to zero, applying the algebra maps $\tau$ and $\phi\otimes\phi$ proves that the negative Serre polynomial maps to zero as well. Together steps 1.2–2.1 show every relation is killed, so [F1] descends $\Delta$ to the quotient. The counit assignment kills the relations directly: each relation becomes either $1=1$ or $0=0$, so it too descends. [given, F1, F2, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Both counit composites and both iterated coproduct composites are algebra homomorphisms, so it suffices by [F2] to check generators. The maps $(\epsilon\otimes1)\Delta$ and $(1\otimes\epsilon)\Delta$ return $L_j,E_i,F_i$ from their displayed formulas. On $L_j$, both iterated coproducts give $L_j\otimes L_j\otimes L_j$; on $E_i$, both give $E_i\otimes K_i\otimes K_i+1\otimes E_i\otimes K_i+1\otimes1\otimes E_i$; on $F_i$, both give $F_i\otimes1\otimes1+K_i^{-1}\otimes F_i\otimes1+K_i^{-1}\otimes K_i^{-1}\otimes F_i$. Hence $\Delta$ is coassociative with counit $\epsilon$. The vector representation of step 1.1 and the iterated coproduct therefore define actions on every $V_N^{\otimes n}$. They are finite sums and products of matrices with entries $0,1,q^{\pm1}$, so all entries lie in $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

lem-hh-quantum-and-hecke-tensor-actions-.facts_and_assumptions_exact:
**Given:** $F=\mathbb Q(q)$, the ordered-basis operator $T$, the quantum generator matrices, and the coproduct of [[def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-centralizers]].

[F1] On a pair of labels, $T$ fixes a repeated label with coefficient $q$, flips an increasing pair, and sends a decreasing pair $(a,b)$ to $(b,a)+c(a,b)$, where $c=q-q^{-1}$ ([[def-hh-hecke-symmetry-and-ordered-basis-operator]]).

[F2] Put $\kappa(a)=\delta_{i,a}-\delta_{i+1,a}$. On two tensor positions the coproduct operators are $\mathcal E_i=E_i\otimes K_i+1\otimes E_i$ and $\mathcal F_i=F_i\otimes1+K_i^{-1}\otimes F_i$; their actions are $\mathcal E_i(a,b)=\delta_{a,i+1}q^{\kappa(b)}(i,b)+\delta_{b,i+1}(a,i)$ and $\mathcal F_i(a,b)=\delta_{a,i}(i+1,b)+q^{-\kappa(a)}\delta_{b,i}(a,i+1)$ ([[def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-centralizers]], [[lem-hh-quantum-presentation-and-tensor-action-descent]]).

[F3] The pair operator preserves the multiset of labels, and $K_i$ is the diagonal combination $L_iL_{i+1}^{-1}$ ([[def-hh-hecke-symmetry-and-ordered-basis-operator]], [[def-hh-type-a-quantum-tensor-action-for-centralizers]]).
lem-hh-quantum-and-hecke-tensor-actions-.proof_exact:
**Given:** The data in [F1]–[F3].

1.1 For each $j$, $L_j\otimes L_j$ acts on $(a,b)$ by the scalar $q^{\delta_{j,a}+\delta_{j,b}}$. Every term in $T(a,b)$ has the same multiset of labels as $(a,b)$, so it has the same scalar. Hence $T(L_j\otimes L_j)=(L_j\otimes L_j)T$; the inverse $L_j^{-1}\otimes L_j^{-1}$ commutes as well. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Fix $i$ and write $(a,b)$ for $e_a\otimes e_b$. If the pair contains no $i+1$, both $T\mathcal E_i$ and $\mathcal E_iT$ vanish by [F2]–[F3]. For the remaining labels, the complete cases are: on $(i+1,i+1)$ both composites give $(i,i+1)+q(i+1,i)$; on $(i+1,i)$ both give $q^2(i,i)$; on $(i,i+1)$ both give $q(i,i)$; for $r<i$, the inputs $(i+1,r)$ and $(r,i+1)$ give respectively $(r,i)+c(i,r)$ and $(i,r)$ under either composite; for $r>i+1$, those same two orientations give respectively $(r,i)$ and $(i,r)+c(r,i)$. These cases exhaust every pair containing $i+1$, including both orientations of each outside label, so $T\mathcal E_i=\mathcal E_iT$. The only coefficient simplification used in the repeated-label case is $q^{-1}+c=q$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 If a pair contains no $i$, both composites with $\mathcal F_i$ vanish. The remaining complete cases are: on $(i,i)$ both give $(i,i+1)+q(i+1,i)$; on $(i,i+1)$ both give $q(i+1,i+1)$; on $(i+1,i)$ both give $q^2(i+1,i+1)$; for $r<i$, the inputs $(i,r)$ and $(r,i)$ give respectively $(r,i+1)+c(i+1,r)$ and $(i+1,r)$ under either composite; for $r>i+1$, they give respectively $(r,i+1)$ and $(i+1,r)+c(r,i+1)$. Thus every pair containing $i$ is covered and $T\mathcal F_i=\mathcal F_iT$. The repeated-label coefficients use $q^{-1}+c=q$ and $1+cq=q^2$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Coassociativity and the coproduct formulas in [F2] give on $n$ positions $\Delta_n(E_i)=\sum_{r=1}^n1^{\otimes(r-1)}\otimes E_i\otimes K_i^{\otimes(n-r)}$, $\Delta_n(F_i)=\sum_{r=1}^n(K_i^{-1})^{\otimes(r-1)}\otimes F_i\otimes1^{\otimes(n-r)}$, and $\Delta_n(L_j)=L_j^{\otimes n}$. For positions $a,a+1$, the two $E_i$ summands at those positions restrict there to $E_i\otimes K_i+1\otimes E_i$, and the two $F_i$ summands restrict to $F_i\otimes1+K_i^{-1}\otimes F_i$; every earlier summand restricts to $K_i\otimes K_i$ or $K_i^{-1}\otimes K_i^{-1}$, and every later summand to the identity. Step 1.1 handles these Cartan factors and steps 1.2–1.3 handle the two-site sums; therefore $T_a$ commutes with each iterated quantum generator. Commuting with the generators implies commuting with their products and linear combinations, which proves $B_F\subseteq\operatorname{End}_{A_F}(V_N^{\otimes n})$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

lem-hh-classical-tensor-centralizer-by-p.definition_or_statement_exact:
Let $N\ge1$, $n\ge1$, $V=\mathbb Q^N$, and $W=V^{\otimes n}$. Let $B_0$ be the image of $\mathbb Q[S_n]$ acting by place permutations, and let $A_0$ be the unital associative subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q}(W)$ generated by
$$\rho_n(a)=\sum_{r=1}^n1^{\otimes(r-1)}\otimes a\otimes1^{\otimes(n-r)},\qquad a\in M_N(\mathbb Q).$$
Then $A_0=\operatorname{End}_{B_0}(W)$. Moreover, $A_0$ is generated already by the operators $\rho_n(E_{i,i+1})$, $\rho_n(E_{i+1,i})$ ($1\le i<N$) and $\rho_n(E_{jj})$ ($1\le j\le N$), where $E_{ab}$ are the matrix units.
lem-hh-classical-tensor-centralizer-by-p.facts_and_assumptions_exact:
**Given:** $N,n\ge1$, the finite-dimensional rational spaces $V,W$, and the actions just defined.

[F1] The matrix units form a basis of $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q}(V)$, and the tensor products of these units form a basis of its $n$-fold tensor power; the canonical map $\operatorname{End}(V)^{\otimes n}\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes n})$ is the isomorphism obtained by its action on elementary tensors ([[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]], [[thm-tensor-product-basis-from-bases]]).

[F2] Conjugation by a place permutation permutes the tensor factors of $\operatorname{End}(V)^{\otimes n}$, and distinct matrix-unit tensors form a basis, as in [F1].

[F3] Operators supported on different tensor positions commute, and $[E_{ab},E_{cd}]=\delta_{bc}E_{ad}-\delta_{da}E_{cb}$ for matrix units.
lem-hh-classical-tensor-centralizer-by-p.proof_exact:
**Given:** The data in [F1]–[F3].

1.1 Under [F1], identify $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q}(W)$ with $M_N(\mathbb Q)^{\otimes n}$. An endomorphism commutes with every place permutation exactly when it is fixed by conjugation by each such permutation. By [F2], this action permutes the tensor-unit basis, so its invariant subspace has as a basis the orbit sums of that basis: invariance says precisely that coefficients are constant on each finite orbit. Thus $\operatorname{End}_{B_0}(W)$ is spanned by the symmetrized tensors of $n$ matrix units. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For any $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in M_N(\mathbb Q)$, multilinear expansion and inclusion–exclusion give $\sum_{J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}(-1)^{n-|J|}(\sum_{j\in J}a_j)^{\otimes n}=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}a_{\sigma(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes a_{\sigma(n)}$. Indeed, a term in the expansion indexed by a function $f:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{1,\ldots,n\}$ occurs with total coefficient $\sum_{J\supseteq\operatorname{im} f}(-1)^{n-|J|}$, which is $1$ when $\operatorname{im}f$ is all of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $0$ otherwise; surjective functions between these equal finite sets are permutations. Taking the $a_j$ to be the matrix units in any multiset orbit makes the right side the orbit sum multiplied by the product of the factorials of its multiplicities. That integer is nonzero and invertible in $\mathbb Q$, so every orbit sum is a rational linear combination of pure powers $a^{\otimes n}$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Fix $a\in M_N(\mathbb Q)$ and put $x_r=1^{\otimes(r-1)}\otimes a\otimes1^{\otimes(n-r)}$. The $x_r$ commute by [F3], and $p_m=\sum_rx_r^m=\rho_n(a^m)\in A_0$. For $E(t)=\prod_{r=1}^n(1+x_rt)=\sum_{m=0}^ne_mt^m$, formal differentiation and $E'(t)/E(t)=\sum_{j\ge1}(-1)^{j-1}p_jt^{j-1}$ give, by comparing coefficients, $m e_m=\sum_{j=1}^m(-1)^{j-1}e_{m-j}p_j$. This induction puts each $e_m$ in $A_0$ because $m$ is invertible in $\mathbb Q$. In particular, $e_n=x_1\cdots x_n=a^{\otimes n}$ belongs to $A_0$. Step 1.2 now gives $\operatorname{End}_{B_0}(W)\subseteq A_0$. Conversely each $\rho_n(a)$ commutes with place permutations because conjugation merely permutes its summands, so $A_0\subseteq\operatorname{End}_{B_0}(W)$ and equality follows. [given, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The map $a\mapsto\rho_n(a)$ is a Lie representation: expanding the commutator, terms in different positions cancel by [F3], leaving $[\rho_n(a),\rho_n(b)]=\rho_n([a,b])$. The adjacent matrix units and the diagonal units generate every matrix unit under brackets: for $r<s$, recursively $E_{r,s}=[E_{r,s-1},E_{s-1,s}]$, and for $r>s$ use $E_{r,s}=[E_{r,r-1},E_{r-1,s}]$; each bracket uses a shorter interval and starts with an adjacent unit, while the $E_{jj}$ supply the diagonal basis. Their $\rho_n$ images therefore generate all $\rho_n(M_N(\mathbb Q))$ as an associative algebra, hence generate $A_0$. [step 2.1, F3, algebra] ∎

lem-hh-finite-semisimple-matrix-double-c.definition_or_statement_exact:
Let $G$ be a finite group, $W$ a finite-dimensional rational representation, and $B\subseteq\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q}(W)$ the image of $\mathbb Q[G]$. Then
$$B=\operatorname{End}_{\operatorname{End}_B(W)}(W).$$
No algebraic-closure, splitting, or commutativity hypothesis on the division algebras of simple summands is required.
lem-hh-finite-semisimple-matrix-double-c.facts_and_assumptions_exact:
**Given:** A finite group $G$, a finite-dimensional left $\mathbb Q[G]$-module $W$, and the finite-complement result below.

[F1] Every submodule of a finite direct sum of simple modules is a direct sum of a subfamily and has a complement; finite-dimensional modules have finite composition series ([[lem-hh-finite-matrix-and-module-preliminaries]]).
lem-hh-finite-semisimple-matrix-double-c.proof_exact:
**Given:** The data in [F1].

1.1 Let $U\subseteq W$ be a $G$-submodule and choose a rational linear projection $p:W\to U$ that is the identity on $U$. The average $P=|G|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}gpg^{-1}$ has image in $U$, restricts to the identity on $U$, and satisfies $hPh^{-1}=P$ for every $h\in G$ by reindexing the finite sum. Thus $P$ is a $G$-linear projection and $\ker P$ complements $U$. Selecting a nonzero submodule of least positive rational dimension makes it simple; splitting it off and inducting on dimension writes $W=\bigoplus_{\lambda}S_\lambda^{m_\lambda}$ with finitely many pairwise nonisomorphic simple modules $S_\lambda$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 For a simple $S$, $D=\operatorname{End}_B(S)$ is a division ring: a nonzero module map has zero kernel and nonzero image, so is bijective and its inverse is again a module map. Give $S$ the right $D^{\mathrm{op}}$-action $s\cdot d^{\mathrm{op}}=d(s)$. It has a finite basis over this division ring: a $D^{\mathrm{op}}$-independent list is rationally independent because $\mathbb Q\,\mathrm{id}_S\subseteq D$, so its length is bounded by $\dim_{\mathbb Q}S$; a list of maximal length spans. Write this basis as $v_1,\ldots,v_d$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The evaluation image $I=\{(bv_1,\ldots,bv_d):b\in B\}\subseteq S^d$ is a $B$-submodule. If it were proper, [F1] would give a nonzero complement; projecting onto one simple summand of that complement and identifying it with $S$ gives a nonzero $B$-map $f:S^d\to S$ that vanishes on $I$. Every such map has the form $f(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\sum_jd_j(x_j)$ with $d_j\in D$. For $b\in B$, $0=f(bv_1,\ldots,bv_d)=b\sum_jd_j(v_j)$, so at $b=1$ one gets $\sum_jv_j\cdot d_j^{\mathrm{op}}=0$. The chosen right $D^{\mathrm{op}}$-basis forces every $d_j=0$, contradicting $f\ne0$. Hence evaluation is onto. Any $D^{\mathrm{op}}$-linear endomorphism of $S$ is therefore the action of some $b\in B$: choose $b$ with the prescribed values on the basis, then both maps are $D^{\mathrm{op}}$-linear and agree on that basis. Thus the image of $B$ on $S$ is $\operatorname{End}_{D^{\mathrm{op}}}(S)$. [given, F1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Apply the same evaluation argument simultaneously to one chosen $D_\lambda^{\mathrm{op}}$-basis of each $S_\lambda$. The target is $X=\bigoplus_\lambda S_\lambda^{d_\lambda}$. If the image of $B\to X$, $b\mapsto(bv_{\lambda,j})_{\lambda,j}$, were proper, [F1] would provide a nonzero $B$-map $f:X\to S_\mu$ killing that image for some simple type $\mu$. A map from $S_\lambda$ to $S_\mu$ is zero for $\lambda\ne\mu$, since a nonzero map between simple modules is an isomorphism; the remaining coordinates of $f$ are maps $d_j\in D_\mu$. Evaluating at $b=1$ contradicts the $D_\mu^{\mathrm{op}}$-independence of the chosen basis of $S_\mu$, exactly as in step 2.1. Therefore every tuple of target values on all these bases is attained by one $b$, and the image of $B$ on the distinct simple types is the full independent product $\prod_\lambda\operatorname{End}_{D_\lambda^{\mathrm{op}}}(S_\lambda)$. [given, F1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 On $W_\lambda=S_\lambda^{m_\lambda}$ this product acts by the same full algebra $R_\lambda=\operatorname{End}_{D_\lambda^{\mathrm{op}}}(S_\lambda)$ on each copy. Its commutant on $S_\lambda$ is exactly $D_\lambda$: a map commutes with $R_\lambda$ iff it commutes with the image of $B$, which is equivalent to being in $\operatorname{End}_B(S_\lambda)$. Hence $\operatorname{End}_B(W)=\bigoplus_\lambda M_{m_\lambda}(D_\lambda)$. To take its commutant on $W_\lambda$, first commute with the diagonal and off-diagonal copy matrix units; this forces zero off-diagonal blocks and the same map $g:S_\lambda\to S_\lambda$ on every diagonal block. Commuting with the diagonal $D_\lambda$ maps is exactly the condition $g(s\cdot d^{\mathrm{op}})=g(s)\cdot d^{\mathrm{op}}$, so $g\in\operatorname{End}_{D_\lambda^{\mathrm{op}}}(S_\lambda)=R_\lambda$. The independent central block projections eliminate maps between distinct $\lambda$. Thus the commutant of $\operatorname{End}_B(W)$ is precisely $\bigoplus_\lambda R_\lambda$ acting diagonally on the multiplicity copies, which is the image of $B$ from step 3.1. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

lem-hh-finite-matrix-rank-under-speciali.definition_or_statement_exact: Let $R=\mathbb Q[q,q^{-1}]_{(q-1)}$, with fraction field $F=\mathbb Q(q)$ and residue field $R/(q-1)\cong\mathbb Q$. If a finite matrix $M$ has entries in $R$, then $\operatorname{rank}_F(M_F)\ge\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Q}(M_{q=1})$. Consequently the kernel dimension of a regularized linear system can only decrease after passing from $q=1$ to $F$. In particular, this applies to finite commutator systems for centralizers. If a finite-dimensional algebra image at $q=1$ is generated by specializations of finitely many regular matrices, finitely many lifted words remain linearly independent over $F$ whenever their specializations form a basis.
lem-hh-finite-matrix-rank-under-speciali.facts_and_assumptions_exact:
**Given:** A finite matrix over the local ring $R$ and, when using the last clause, a finite-dimensional matrix algebra generated by a finite family of regular matrices.

[F1] Rank–nullity holds for finite matrices over each of the fields $\mathbb Q$ and $F$, and determinants are polynomial in their entries ([[lem-hh-finite-matrix-and-module-preliminaries]]).

[F2] Vectorizing a finite square matrix identifies its entries with coordinates in a finite-dimensional vector space, so commutators with a finite set of matrices form a finite matrix of linear equations.
lem-hh-finite-matrix-rank-under-speciali.proof_exact:
**Given:** The data in [F1]–[F2].

1.1 If $r=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Q}(M_{q=1})$ is zero, the desired rank inequality is immediate. If $r>0$, choose $r$ independent columns of the specialized matrix. Gaussian elimination on that $m\times r$ submatrix shows its row space also has dimension $r$, so choose $r$ independent rows; the resulting square submatrix is invertible and has nonzero determinant by [[cor-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-is-a-unit]]. Conversely a nonzero $r\times r$ minor gives $r$ independent columns. Thus some $r\times r$ minor of $M_{q=1}$ has determinant nonzero in the residue field. Its determinant in $R$ specializes to that nonzero value, so it is a nonzero element of $R$ and remains nonzero in its fraction field $F$. Hence $\operatorname{rank}_F(M_F)\ge r$. Since both matrices have the same number of columns, rank–nullity gives $\dim_F\ker(M_F)\le\dim_{\mathbb Q}\ker(M_{q=1})$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For regular endomorphisms $g_1(q),\ldots,g_s(q)$ of a fixed finite free tensor space, vectorize $X$ and form the finite matrix of $X\mapsto([X,g_1(q)],\ldots,[X,g_s(q)])$. Its kernel is exactly the simultaneous commutant of the $g_i$, which equals the commutant of the algebra they generate. Applying step 1.1 bounds the generic commutant dimension above by the specialized commutant dimension. This argument uses only the selected regular matrices; it does not specialize arbitrary rational functions. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $A_0$ be the specialized image, generated by the specialized finite family, in an endomorphism space of finite dimension. The set of all words in those generators spans $A_0$; from this spanning set choose a finite subset that is a basis, by adding a word only when it increases the dimension, which can happen at most $\dim A_0$ times. If $\dim A_0=0$, the image lower bound is immediate; otherwise the same words in the regular lifts form a matrix over $R$ whose specialization has full column rank. Step 1.1, applied to a nonzero square minor of that column matrix, shows the lifted words are $F$-linearly independent. Hence the generic image dimension is at least $\dim_{\mathbb Q}A_0$. The argument is identical for any other finite regular generating family. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Let $A_0$ be the unital algebra generated by the classical operators $\rho_n(a)$ of [[lem-hh-classical-tensor-centralizer-by-polarization]], and let $B_0$ be the place-permutation image of $\mathbb Q[S_n]$. The regular quantum and Hecke matrix families below specialize to generating families for these two rational algebras. Then
$$\dim_{\mathbb Q}A_0\le\dim_F A_F,\qquad \dim_{\mathbb Q}B_0\le\dim_F B_F,$$
$$\dim_F\operatorname{End}_{B_F}(M_F)\le\dim_{\mathbb Q}A_0,\qquad \dim_F\operatorname{End}_{A_F}(M_F)\le\dim_{\mathbb Q}B_0.$$
These are separate image lower bounds and commutant upper bounds; the commuting inclusion needed to turn them into equalities is proved in [[lem-hh-quantum-and-hecke-tensor-actions-commute]].
lem-hh-classical-and-generic-tensor-doub.facts_and_assumptions_exact:
**Given:** The quantum and Hecke actions above, their local relation-descent proofs, and the three local rank/centralizer suppliers below.

[F1] The specialized classical quantum image satisfies $A_0=\operatorname{End}_{B_0}(M_0)$ ([[lem-hh-classical-tensor-centralizer-by-polarization]]).

[F2] Over $\mathbb Q$, the finite permutation image satisfies $B_0=\operatorname{End}_{A_0}(M_0)$ ([[lem-hh-finite-semisimple-matrix-double-commutant]]).

[F3] A finite matrix over $\mathbb Q[q,q^{-1}]_{(q-1)}$ has generic rank at least its rank at $q=1$; this gives both word-image lower bounds and commutant-kernel upper bounds ([[lem-hh-finite-matrix-rank-under-specialization]]).
lem-hh-classical-and-generic-tensor-doub.proof_exact:
**Given:** The data in [F1]–[F3].

1.1 Put $R=\mathbb Q[q,q^{-1}]_{(q-1)}$ and $M_R=(R^N)^{\otimes n}$, a finite free module with fraction-field fiber $M_F$ and residue-field fiber $M_0$. All Hecke matrices and all iterated quantum matrices are regular over $R$ by their explicit formulas. For the quantum family, also use $H_j=(L_j-I)/(q-1)$. On a basis word with $m_j$ occurrences of $j$, $L_j$ has eigenvalue $q^{m_j}$, so $H_j$ is the diagonal matrix with entry $1+q+\cdots+q^{m_j-1}$ if $m_j>0$ and $0$ if $m_j=0$. Thus $H_j$ is regular and specializes to the classical diagonal count operator $\rho_n(E_{jj})$. The generators $E_i,F_i,H_j$ specialize to the adjacent matrix Lie operators and all diagonal count operators, which generate $A_0$ by the last conclusion of [[lem-hh-classical-tensor-centralizer-by-polarization]]; $L_j^{\pm1}$ specialize to the identity. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 In a basis of $M_R$, vectorize $X\in\operatorname{End}(M_R)$. The simultaneous commutator system for the finite family $T_1,\ldots,T_{n-1}$ is a finite matrix over $R$, and its kernel over $F$ is $\operatorname{End}_{B_F}(M_F)$ while its kernel at $q=1$ is $\operatorname{End}_{B_0}(M_0)$. By [F3] its generic kernel dimension is at most the specialized one, which equals $\dim_{\mathbb Q}A_0$ by [F1]. The same construction for the finite family $E_i,F_i,L_j^{\pm1},H_j$ has generic kernel $\operatorname{End}_{A_F}(M_F)$; at $q=1$ the family generates $A_0$, so its specialized kernel is $\operatorname{End}_{A_0}(M_0)$, of dimension $\dim_{\mathbb Q}B_0$ by [F2]. This proves both commutant upper bounds independently. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The algebra $A_0$ is finite-dimensional and generated by the specializations at $q=1$ of the regular quantum family in step 1.1. Words in that finite family span it, so select a finite word basis. The same words in the regular generic matrices have a vectorized-column matrix over $R$ whose specialization has full column rank; [F3] gives their $F$-linear independence. Hence $\dim_F A_F\ge\dim_{\mathbb Q}A_0$. Words in the finite family $T_1,\ldots,T_{n-1}$ similarly specialize to a spanning family of $B_0$; selecting a basis and applying [F3] gives $\dim_F B_F\ge\dim_{\mathbb Q}B_0$. Only these chosen regular words are specialized; no arbitrary rational denominator is evaluated at $q=1$. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

thm-hh-generic-quantum-schur-weyl-mutual.definition_or_statement_exact:
Let $F=\mathbb Q(q)$, $N\ge1$, $n\ge0$, $M=(F^N)^{\otimes n}$, and let $A_F,B_F\subseteq\operatorname{End}_F(M)$ be the images of the quantum and normalized Hecke tensor actions defined above. Then
$$A_F=\operatorname{End}_{B_F}(M),\qquad B_F=\operatorname{End}_{A_F}(M).$$
These are equalities for the two matrix-algebra images. If $N<n$, no faithfulness of the abstract Hecke algebra is asserted. If $N\ge n$, the abstract Hecke action is faithful. The theorem is only over the rational function field $\mathbb Q(q)$ and asserts no equality at a root of unity, at an arbitrary specialized parameter, or over a field of positive characteristic.
thm-hh-generic-quantum-schur-weyl-mutual.facts_and_assumptions_exact:
**Given:** $F=\mathbb Q(q)$, integers $N\ge1,n\ge0$, the local commuting inclusion, the rank bounds, and the abstract Hecke standard basis.

[F1] The two images commute: $B_F\subseteq\operatorname{End}_{A_F}(M)$ and $A_F\subseteq\operatorname{End}_{B_F}(M)$ ([[lem-hh-quantum-and-hecke-tensor-actions-commute]]).

[F2] For $N\ge2,n\ge1$, the two generic image lower bounds and commutant upper bounds are those of [[lem-hh-classical-and-generic-tensor-double-centralizer-suppliers]].

[F3] The abstract type-A Hecke algebra has basis $\{t_w:w\in S_n\}$ over $F$, obtained by base change from the universal standard-basis theorem ([[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]], [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]]).

[F4] A nonzero minor of a matrix with entries regular at $q=1$ remains nonzero over $F=\mathbb Q(q)$ ([[lem-hh-finite-matrix-rank-under-specialization]]).
thm-hh-generic-quantum-schur-weyl-mutual.proof_exact:
**Given:** The data in [F1]–[F4].

1.1 Suppose first $N\ge2$ and $n\ge1$. By [F2] and the commuting inclusions [F1], $\dim_{\mathbb Q}A_0\le\dim_F A_F\le\dim_F\operatorname{End}_{B_F}(M)\le\dim_{\mathbb Q}A_0$, so every inequality is equality and $A_F=\operatorname{End}_{B_F}(M)$ because the included finite-dimensional subspaces have equal dimension. The other sandwich is $\dim_{\mathbb Q}B_0\le\dim_F B_F\le\dim_F\operatorname{End}_{A_F}(M)\le\dim_{\mathbb Q}B_0$, which gives $B_F=\operatorname{End}_{A_F}(M)$ by the same inclusion-and-dimension argument. This establishes both mutual centralizer equalities without generic semisimplicity or a character formula. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Assume $N\ge n\ge1$. On $v=e_1\otimes\cdots\otimes e_n$, the orbit vectors $\rho_n(t_w)v$ have entries regular at $q=1$; their specializations are the $n!$ distinct tensors obtained by permuting the distinct basis labels. Their vectorized column matrix therefore has an $n!\times n!$ minor equal to $1$ at $q=1$, which remains nonzero over $F$ by [F4]. Thus the orbit vectors are linearly independent over $F$. If $h=\sum_{w\in S_n}a_wt_w$ lies in the kernel, the standard basis [F3] gives this expansion and $0=\rho_n(h)v=\sum_wa_w\rho_n(t_w)v$ forces every $a_w=0$. Hence the abstract action is faithful. [given, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 If $n=0$, then $M=F$ and both unital images and both commutants are $F$; the unique unital map from the abstract algebra $H_0=F$ is the identity, so this action is faithful. If $N=1$, $M$ is one-dimensional; the quantum image contains the scalars and every Hecke generator acts by $q$, so both images and both commutants are again $F$. These direct cases cover the parameters excluded from step 1.1. [given, F1, algebra]

3.1 In the range $N<n$ the equalities in step 1.1 remain image equalities and do not identify $B_F$ with the abstract Hecke algebra. The distinction is real: for $N=1,n=2$, the abstract algebra has basis $1,t_1$ by [F3], while its one-dimensional tensor-space action sends $t_1$ to $q$; the nonzero element $t_1-q$ is in the kernel. No claim of faithfulness in the full range $N<n$ is used in either centralizer equality. [step 2.1, step 1.1, F3, algebra] ∎
